name: Genioplasty

lead: Genioplasty is surgery to change chin projection, height or width, usually by cutting and sliding the lower jaw border, or by adding an implant.
It is a long-established oral surgery procedure and a frequent topic on looksmax.org, where users weigh it against bimaxillary surgery.

paras: In a sliding genioplasty a segment of the chin bone is cut, moved forward, back or vertically, and fixed with a titanium plate; implants add volume instead.
Reported effects include swelling, temporary or lasting numbness of the lip and chin, infection and implant displacement. It is performed under general anaesthesia when bone is cut.

lead: Genioplasty is chin surgery that changes the size, shape or projection of the chin. The term is used for operations that move or reshape the chin bone, most commonly a sliding genioplasty in which the lower border of the mandible is cut and repositioned, and it is also used more loosely for chin augmentation with implants.[1] Surgeons who perform it include oral and maxillofacial surgeons, plastic surgeons and otolaryngologists.[1]

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as one of the more commonly considered facial bone procedures, often as an alternative or complement to double-jaw (bimaxillary) surgery for a recessed chin, and members debate how many millimetres of advancement to seek.[2][3] The published literature consists mainly of surgical technique papers, accuracy studies of computer-planned surgery and registered trials of fixation and implant methods; no registry entry or study in this literature evaluates the looksmaxxing claims directly.[4][5]
infobox: Oral and maxillofacial, plastic and ENT surgeons

paras: A sliding genioplasty cuts a horseshoe-shaped segment from the lower border of the mandible and moves it forward to increase projection or backward to reduce it, then fixes it in place with a titanium plate and screws.[1] Related bone-based approaches include the T-osteotomy, developed by Korean surgeons, which is described as narrowing and lengthening the chin.[1] Alternatively, implants made of silicone, porous polyethylene or other materials can add projection, usually placed through the mouth, and injectable fillers are a temporary non-surgical option.[1]
Genioplasty is also performed together with other jaw operations. Reviews of orthognathic surgery describe chin repositioning as one component of planning in patients with jaw discrepancies.[6]

Early descriptions of chin reshaping appear in the 1950s oral surgery literature, including papers on correcting mandibular prognathism and retrognathia with consideration of genioplasty.[7][8] Computer-aided planning with patient-specific guides and plates has been studied since the 2010s.[9]

Wikipedia notes that bone-based augmentation usually gives a larger correction than implants and that results from implants and bone surgery are generally lasting.[1] A prospective multicentre study of 65 orthognathic patients examined how closely computer-planned outcomes, including chin repositioning, matched postoperative results.[9]

Common effects include swelling, bruising and temporary lip or chin numbness; less common ones include infection, nerve damage and implant displacement.[1] A study of 1,034 orthognathic patients examined at two years assessed sensation in the mental nerve region after mandibular osteotomies including genioplasty and reported that rates of neurosensory deficiency differed by procedure.[10]

Registered trials mainly compare surgical methods rather than the appearance outcomes claimed in forums. They include a comparison of box and mini-wing genioplasty techniques (n=40),[4] studies of patient-specific titanium or PEEK plates and implants for accuracy,[11][12][13] a comparison of a custom alloplastic implant with computer-guided genioplasty at one year,[14] a trial of advancement genioplasty with or without submental liposuction,[15] and a trial of electroacupuncture for numbness and swelling after orthognathic surgery and mentoplasty (n=118).[16] Many are small and several have unknown status.

Forum users post profile photos and ask whether a genioplasty or bimaxillary surgery would suit them, and discuss surgeon-quoted advancement figures such as 4-5 mm for an average chin.[2][3] Some posters describe it as a high-impact procedure that can be combined with fillers or rhinoplasty, while others in the same threads advise that a given profile does not need surgery.[3][17]

Aufricht reports combined nose and chin surgery.[1]
The T-osteotomy technique is described by Korean surgeons.[1]
Trials of computer-guided, patient-specific genioplasty plates and implants begin.[11][12][13]
